```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("_setup.R")
library(bayesmokken)
```

```{r fit, include = FALSE}
data(srs)
fit <- bb_mokken_h(srs, draws = 2000, seed = 1)
iv <- bm_interval(fit)
```

This vignette covers the binary path: how the interval is generated, why it
needed correcting, and why the correction's constant is not an argument.
Notation follows `vignette("m1-foundations")`.

## The Bayesian bootstrap

Draw a weight vector for the $n$ respondents from a flat Dirichlet
[@rubin_bayesian_1981],

$$(w_1, \dots, w_n) \sim \mathrm{Dirichlet}(1, \dots, 1),$$

recompute $H$ under those weights, and repeat $B$ times. The resulting spread
of $H$ values is the sampling variability the interval describes.

```{r draws}
d <- bm_draws(fit, what = "scale")
data.frame(draws = length(d), mean = mean(d), sd = sd(d))
```

### Pattern grouping is an implementation, not a method

With binary items, many respondents share a response pattern, and $H$ depends
on the data only through the pattern frequencies. The implementation therefore
draws weights over *patterns* rather than over rows. This is a sparsity
optimisation with no effect on the distribution being sampled — aggregating
Dirichlet coordinates over a partition yields a Dirichlet with summed
parameters, which is exactly the pattern-level law.

```{r patterns}
c(respondents = iv$n_complete,
  distinct_patterns = nrow(unique(srs[stats::complete.cases(srs), ])))
```

Where it shows is speed: this fit resamples
`r nrow(unique(srs[stats::complete.cases(srs), ]))` patterns rather than
`r iv$n_complete` rows on every draw.

## Why the raw interval needed correcting

The first-order argument is local, not global. With a fixed declared item set,
strictly ordered interior marginal probabilities, maximum-covariance
denominators separated from zero, and a positive finite influence-function
variance, $H$ is a smooth functional and admits an influence-function
expansion. On that **regular domain**, the Bayesian bootstrap's conditional law
agrees with the sampling law to first order [@lo_large_1987]. Tied margins,
support boundaries, and vanishing denominators are outside that smooth-domain
statement; at a tie the relevant functional may instead be piecewise smooth.

The theory establishes an order statement: changing an interval-width
multiplier by $O(n^{-1/2})$ perturbs its endpoints by $O_p(n^{-1})$, so the
first-order law is preserved. It does **not** determine whether the raw
interval should widen or shrink, nor does it derive the functional form or the
constant below. The observed finite-sample shortfall, the widening direction,
and $\gamma=0.25$ came from the prespecified train–validate–confirm simulation
program.

## The correction

Let $m$ be the midpoint of the raw interval and $w$ its half-width. The
calibrated interval is

$$\left[\, m - \kappa_n w,\ \; m + \kappa_n w \,\right],
\qquad \kappa_n = 1 + \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{n}}, \qquad \gamma = 0.25 .$$

**Executable consistency check — reconstruct endpoints from exported raw
draws, raw-data $n$, literal $0.25$, and type-8 quantiles.**

```{r verify-calibration}
raw_q <- stats::quantile(d, c(0.025, 0.975), type = 8,
                         names = FALSE, na.rm = TRUE)
complete_n <- nrow(srs[stats::complete.cases(srs), , drop = FALSE])
m <- mean(raw_q)
w <- diff(raw_q) / 2
kappa <- 1 + 0.25 / sqrt(complete_n)
expected <- c(lower = m - kappa * w, upper = m + kappa * w)

stopifnot(
  identical(complete_n, iv$n_complete),
  isTRUE(all.equal(raw_q, c(iv$raw_lower, iv$raw_upper),
                   tolerance = 1e-12)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(expected, c(lower = iv$lower, upper = iv$upper),
                   tolerance = 1e-12))
)
c(midpoint = m, kappa = kappa, expected)
```

Three properties follow from that form and are enforced rather than merely
intended:

**The midpoint never moves.** The correction changes length only. A shift would
be a different kind of claim, and none is made.

**No clipping.** If an endpoint falls outside $[-1, 1]$ it is reported where it
falls. Clipping would silently improve the appearance of coverage at exactly
the configurations where the method is under most strain.

**No method cascade.** One method is applied, always. A procedure that fell
back to an alternative when the first looked unsatisfactory would have coverage
properties nobody measured.

```{r frozen}
c(gamma = iv$gamma, clipping = iv$endpoint_clipping,
  cascade = iv$per_replication_method_cascade, level = iv$level)
```

The multiplier shrinks with $n$, as an $n^{-1/2}$ term must:

```{r fig-calibration, fig.alt = "Width multiplier for the binary correction against sample size, starting near 1.08 at n = 10 and decaying toward 1 as n grows."}
bm_plot_calibration(mode = "binary")
```

## Why $\gamma$ is not an argument

$\gamma = 0.25$ was selected on training conditions, evaluated once on held-out
conditions, and then confirmed prospectively on a fresh simulation — so it was
never tuned on the data used to evaluate it. That sequence is what licenses the
coverage claim, and it licenses it **for this value only**.

Exposing $\gamma$ would invite users to vary it, and the coverage of any other
value is simply unmeasured. So the constant is frozen and unreachable:

```{r no-gamma, error = TRUE}
bb_mokken_h(srs, draws = 200, seed = 1, gamma = 0.5)
```

The confidence level is frozen for the same reason:

```{r no-level, error = TRUE}
bb_mokken_h(srs, draws = 200, seed = 1, level = 0.90)
```

If you want the uncorrected interval, it remains available under its own name,
labelled as making no calibrated claim:

```{r equal-tail}
raw <- bb_mokken_h(srs, draws = 2000, seed = 1, interval = "equal_tail")
bm_interval(raw)$method_id
```

## Quantile type and defined draws

The endpoints are type-8 sample quantiles, which is a fixed choice rather than
R's default:

**Partial independent check — base R recomputes the two quantile types from
the exported draw vector.**

```{r verify-quantile}
q8 <- stats::quantile(d, c(0.025, 0.975), type = 8, names = FALSE)
q7 <- stats::quantile(d, c(0.025, 0.975), type = 7, names = FALSE)

stopifnot(all.equal(q8, c(iv$raw_lower, iv$raw_upper), tolerance = 1e-12))
rbind(`type 8 (used)` = q8, `type 7 (R default)` = q7,
      `in the object` = c(iv$raw_lower, iv$raw_upper))
```

Type 8 reproduces the stored endpoints to `r format(max(abs(q8 - c(iv$raw_lower, iv$raw_upper))), scientific = TRUE, digits = 2)`,
while type 7 differs in the fourth decimal. The difference is small but it is
not nothing, and pinning the type is what makes the endpoints reproducible
across machines.

A draw whose denominator vanishes gives an undefined coefficient. Those are
counted, and the interval requires enough defined draws before it will report:

```{r defined}
c(defined = iv$defined_draws, total = iv$total_draws,
  minimum = iv$minimum_defined_draws)
```

For the binary path the minimum is $\max(100, \lceil 0.90 B \rceil)$:

**Executable consistency check — stored draw counts obey the declared
minimum formula.**

```{r verify-minimum}
stopifnot(iv$minimum_defined_draws == max(100, ceiling(0.90 * iv$total_draws)))
```

Falling short is a failure, not a smaller sample. An interval computed from
whichever draws happened to be defined would describe a conditional
distribution nobody specified.

## The evidence

The binary article evaluates the interval in two stages on the same 32
population laws, drawn from four data-generating families chosen to strain the
statistic in different ways (latent monotone conditional independence,
heterogeneous-margin target control, asymmetric-quality nonexchangeable items,
and controlled local dependence). Undefined intervals count as misses
throughout.

**The confirmatory stage** ran 108,000 replications under rules fixed in
advance and met all 9 prespecified acceptance criteria. In the 22 regular
cells the calibrated interval covered **94.5% – 95.1%** by family, against
94.0% – 94.6% for the raw equal-tail interval it widens, at a mean-length cost
of 2.46% – 2.65%.

**The paired comparison** then drew fresh samples from the same laws and
computed six standard intervals on every one of them. Coverage over the 22
regular cells, averaged over the four families:

| Interval | Coverage at nominal 95% |
|---|---|
| **Calibrated BB (this package's default)** | **94.8%** (families 94.5% – 95.0%) |
| Raw equal-tail BB | 94.4% |
| Nonparametric bootstrap, percentile | 94.6% |
| Nonparametric bootstrap, BCa | 95.3% |
| `mokken` delta-method Wald | 94.1% |
| `mokken` range-preserving | 94.2% |

The calibrated interval gained **0.41** percentage points over the raw interval
(Monte Carlo standard error 0.02) at a mean-length cost of 2.46% – 2.65%. The
BCa interval covered more, with longer intervals, and neither was uniformly
closer to nominal across families. Versions of the delta-method and BCa
constructions screened for regularity, which return no interval at empirical
margin ties, covered as little as 71.4% by family; the article reports them as
a diagnostic, not as comparators.

The reason to prefer the calibrated interval is not that it is Bayesian, or
newer. It is that its coverage was measured, prospectively, under a rule fixed
in advance, and then checked against the intervals already in use.
